title: Competitor 100x larger, yet overtaken in downloads: scale is not a moat
dek: A founder with no email background overtook downloads through product experience, while Twilio—inventor of DevRel—acquired SendGrid but left it dormant.
why: The founder discusses concrete engineering details: IP pools, MCP permission models, changes to AI search pages—relevant for anyone building developer-first products or managing growth influenced by AI recommendations.
who: Founders building developer-first products, engineers concerned with email/sending infrastructure, and marketers experimenting with AEO growth.
skip: Around 31:00, a low-density discussion of SMS, WhatsApp, and phone channels; can be skipped.

points.h: Once thought beating SendGrid impossible, now doubling his lead
points.body: Zeno Rocha recalls early fears SendGrid was ‘impossible’ to beat. This year, Resend's npm downloads surpassed SendGrid—now more than double. Resend serves 4.3M users, just crossed 120k+ paying customers including Warner Brothers and HBO, plus a Japanese group that purchased ~20k domains in one transaction.

points.h: Trust users first, police behavior after, not before
points.body: Most email providers require signup forms and 2-day manual review, rejecting most applications. Zeno rejects this model: instead of imprisoning users for eighteen years before proving they deserve freedom, he flips it. Default trust, then immediately block on hard signals like bounce rates and complaints—since most issues stem from misuse, not abuse.

points.h: A hundred times larger, yet unable to win with scale
points.body: Twilio was 100x Resend's size at the start, yet couldn't crush it through scale. The conversation landed on a judgment: commodity businesses like email have no scale advantage. Product quality is all that matters. Twilio, which invented DevRel, now appears to coast on past laurels, underinvesting in SendGrid and SMS.

points.h: From leasing AWS SES to owning the entire sending stack
points.body: Resend started on AWS SES, differentiating on developer UX. Now building in-house: acquiring and managing IP pools, establishing carrier relationships, switching email delivery from Node.js to Go for speed. The goal is finer observability—previously the platform couldn't see whether a sent email reached the inbox, spam folder, or promotions tab.

points.h: One MCP forced a complete rebuild of permission systems
points.body: Resend's first MCP was a local version written part-time by Yoko, an a16z investor. Growth demanded a remote MCP, but that required OAuth and RBAC first. They redesigned the entire account permissions system from scratch, only then moving to distribution and the official plugin marketplace.

points.h: Eighty tools didn't confuse the model; data density did
points.body: The industry feared many MCP tools would confuse models; Cloudflare even capped theirs at two. Resend went opposite: ~20 at launch, now 80+. Tool quantity itself hasn't caused confusion. The real issue is single calls returning too much data, losing information. Achieving feature parity with the dashboard—billing, team invites, account deletion—is extremely hard.

points.h: AI miscalculated pricing, so he copied the price list to markdown
points.body: Zeno asked AI to compare Resend against competitors' cost for 1.2M emails—the numbers came back wrong, and the model claimed Resend ‘pricing is opaque’. The problem: AI won't execute JavaScript calculator widgets on the page. Fix: duplicate the numbers as plain text in a markdown version of the same page. Fixed in days, but now maintaining two content sources with no single source of truth.

points.h: Better a smaller company his daughter actually wants to spend time with
points.body: A YC partner told Zeno his design perfectionism was slowing progress—it stung, but was fair. He clarified his priorities: in ten years, he'd rather have $10M revenue and a daughter who wants to play with him than $100M and a distant relationship. He carried this priority back into parenting decisions.
